units.passage: This policy pertains to the use of tools that may rely on current or future technologies that do not (or make it impossible to) adhere to standards that CDS expects its own students and faculty to uphold with respect to appropriation of others work and proper attribution. The policy should not be construed as endorsing this practice.
units.why: "tools that may rely on ... technologies that do not (or make it impossible to) adhere to standards that CDS expects ... appropriation of others work and proper attribution" flags attribution/IP concerns about AI tools, P52.

units.passage: cannot be reused verbatim in later documents even when the words are the researcher's own
units.policy: Prior work published under a copyright transfer (IEEE, ACM, Elsevier, Springer) cannot be reused verbatim in later documents even when the words are the researcher's own; AI assistance does not change this.
units.why: Prior published work 'cannot be reused verbatim in later documents even when the words are the researcher's own' and 'AI assistance does not change this': a copyright and ownership rule (P52).
units.fit_note: Concerns self-plagiarism and copyright transfer, with AI making no difference.

units.passage: the organization generally acquires ownership of the contents (through a copyright agreement.)
units.policy: When a student publishes under a professional society such as IEEE, the organization generally acquires ownership of the contents through a copyright agreement, so re-used text can be flagged by a plagiarism checker even though the words are the student's own.
units.why: The handbook explains that journals and societies such as IEEE acquire ownership of published text, so reusing it can trigger plagiarism checkers (P52).
units.fit_note: Concerns self-plagiarism and copyright transfer rather than AI output.

units.passage: Lecture notes made available to you are the intellectual property of the course developer/instructor
units.why: "Lecture notes ... are the intellectual property of the course developer/instructor ... protected by copyright law" states an IP fact behind the upload ban: P52.

units.passage: Violating intellectual property laws.
units.why: Students may be penalized for "Violating intellectual property laws." P52.
units.fit_note: States a penalty for IP violations, not guidance on AI outputs. Lists IP violation as a penalizable act without detail.

units.passage: Students should be made aware that current copyright regulations around generative-AI-produced content are unclear. Copyright violations might also occur when AI supplies text from unattributed sources. Additionally, future detection tools might point towards generative-AI-sourced text that was inaccurately documented by the student author. Limitations regarding future publication may arise. Thus, caution is urged for all students when using generative AI in the composition of their manuscripts.
units.why: "current copyright regulations around generative-AI-produced content are unclear" and AI may supply text "from unattributed sources"; a copyright and ownership caution, P52.

units.passage: Copyright violations might also occur when AI supplies text from unattributed sources.
units.why: "Copyright violations might also occur when AI supplies text from unattributed sources." Copyright risk of AI output, P52.

units.passage: Entering unpublished or proprietary research information into unapproved AI tools may constitute disclosure to a third party and could affect intellectual property, confidentiality, or contractual protections.
units.why: "Entering unpublished or proprietary research information into unapproved AI tools may constitute disclosure to a third party and could affect intellectual property". IP consequence, P52.

units.passage: Overall, how the use of AI impacts the domains of patent applications, copyright licensing, and trademarks is unclear.
units.why: 'how the use of AI impacts the domains of patent applications, copyright licensing, and trademarks is unclear' - open IP questions (P52).

units.passage: At present, the person entering the prompts and text materials retains the copyright.
units.why: 'At present, the person entering the prompts and text materials retains the copyright' - a fact about ownership of AI inputs and outputs (P52).

units.passage: The use of patented or copyrighted material as a prompt for the AI may compromise claim or security of those materials.
units.why: It warns that using 'patented or copyrighted material as a prompt' may 'compromise claim or security' of it. This is a caution about inputs, not a ban, so P52 partly fits.
units.fit_note: Warns about inputs rather than output ownership; it is not a rule against uploading.

units.passage: Students disclose their intellectual property when uploading to public AI chatbots.
units.why: 'Students disclose their intellectual property when uploading to public AI chatbots' warns about IP exposure; closest type is P52 (ownership and licensing of inputs).
units.fit_note: Warns that uploading to public chatbots exposes IP; it does not discuss copyright or licensing of output. (Coder B: Warns that uploading to public chatbots discloses the student's IP; not about copyright or licensing of output.)

units.passage: The companies behind generative AI tools train them on large language models (LLMs) that contain some content that infringes on copyright and is used without consent.
units.why: The passage says training data "infringes on copyright and is used without consent", an intellectual-property concern about AI; P52 (copyright and licensing of AI) fits and it is informational.
units.fit_note: Concerns copyright of training data rather than of inputs or outputs.

units.passage: Any copyrighted, proprietary, research, educational, or non-public information provided to Generative AI may be stored on servers not controlled by the University of Alaska and could potentially be shared with third parties.
units.why: Copyrighted or non-public information given to AI 'may be stored on servers not controlled by' UA; IP risk of inputs (P52).
units.fit_note: Warns about exposure of IP; no rule is stated.

units.passage: Before using Generative AI, make sure to read, understand, and follow the platform’s terms of service, privacy policies, and any supplemental AI data agreements.
units.why: 'Before using Generative AI, make sure to read, understand, and follow the platform's terms of service, privacy policies, and any supplemental AI data agreements.' It is advice in the risk-awareness section (not a 'must' sentence) about terms of use, so P52 with should; the timing is when starting to use a tool, so during-work.
units.fit_note: Covers terms of service generally, including legal exposure, not only ownership of output.

units.passage: University employees and students are prohibited from using Generative AI to reverse engineer, decompile, and/or develop competing AI models except as permitted by law or applicable licensing terms.
units.why: Users 'are prohibited from using Generative AI to reverse engineer, decompile, and/or develop competing AI models'; P52 since the exception turns on licensing terms (P74 targets deception or malice).
units.fit_note: Bans a specific use of AI against model owners; not about ownership of outputs. | A prohibition tied to licensing terms rather than ownership of outputs.

units.passage: Generative AI-produced content may be biased, inaccurate, completely fabricated or contain copyright-protected or proprietary information, therefore requiring thorough human review prior to use.
units.policy: Generative AI-produced content may contain copyright-protected or proprietary information.
units.why: The same sentence warns output may "contain copyright-protected or proprietary information"; a distinct IP concern, P52 (not P31, which is about accuracy).

units.passage: The use ofintellectual property by large language models is debated; lawsuits about infringement on intellectualproperty rights are pending.
units.why: The guide notes 'The use of intellectual property by large language models is debated; lawsuits ... are pending', a copyright and IP concern (P52).

units.passage: Plagiarism rules apply to AI outputs: if any user incorporates text, code, images, or data produced by an AI, they must ensure that doing so does not violate any copyrights or intellectual property rights, and they should cite or credit sources as required (
units.why: Users incorporating AI output 'must ensure that doing so does not violate any copyrights or intellectual property rights', a rule on copyright of AI output, P52.

units.passage: Copyrighted data or information may only be uploaded into a non-licensed University approved AI tool with permission of the copyright holder or in limited use that follows Fair Use laws and policies.
units.why: Copyrighted data 'may only be uploaded into a non-licensed University approved AI tool with permission of the copyright holder or in limited use that follows Fair Use'. Copyright rule, P52.

units.passage: Otherwise, a licensed University approved tool is required.
units.why: 'Otherwise, a licensed University approved tool is required' for copyrighted material, tying copyright to licensed tools. P52.

units.passage: Be aware that the texts and images produced solely by GAI prompts are currently not protected by U.S. copyright law.
units.why: The policy warns that 'texts and images produced solely by GAI prompts are currently not protected by U.S. copyright law'. A fact about ownership of AI output, so P52.

units.passage: Use of AI-based tools must not violate any copyright or intellectual property laws (please refer to UAMS Distribution of Royalties from Inventions UAMS Academic Affairs Policy – 2.1.6 4 policy; U of A Board Patent and Copyright Policy; and U of A Board Copyright and Distance Learning Policy).
units.why: 'Use of AI-based tools must not violate any copyright or intellectual property laws' is a rule on lawful use, which is P52 (copyright); P77 would fit too but the content is copyright.

units.passage: Users are responsible for ensuring GAI outputs do not infringe third-party rights; indemnification risk lies with the requester absent a vendor contractual defense.
units.why: 'Users are responsible for ensuring GAI outputs do not infringe third-party rights' assigns infringement responsibility to the user, a copyright rule, so P52.

units.passage: Additionally, users must comply with copyright and intellectual property laws, avoid infringement, and guarantee that all content meets legal standards.
units.why: Reconciled coding for "users must comply with copyright and intellectual property laws, avoid infringement": Coder A coded require, coder B restrict. The sentence only says users 'must comply with copyright and intellectual property laws', a legal-compliance duty that neither requires nor restricts AI use. Final neutral, as for other P52 units.

units.passage: The use of an AI system must be disclosed to capture institutional knowledge. For example, if AI is used to create code and included in a larger section of code, there must be documentation as to which code section is AI -derived and who reviewed it. Disclosure should be considered when using AI in much the same way as citing a source in writing. f. The use of an AI system must comply with any terms of use or contractual limitations. Users should have all terms or use or contracts for AI systems reviewed by the Legal Department to ensure compliance with contractual obligations in using an AI system.
units.policy: The use of an AI system must comply with any terms of use or contractual limitations.
units.why: Reconciled coding for "must comply with any terms of use or contractual limitations": Coder A coded require and merged two rules in the policy text; coder B coded restrict. The anchor sentence is a compliance duty (neutral); the separate sentence about Legal Department review is kept as its own unit (only coder B). Policy text narrowed to the one rule.

units.passage: AI outputs can sometimes resemble copyrighted material, leading to potential legal concerns.
units.why: "AI outputs can sometimes resemble copyrighted material" raises IP risk, P52, informs.

units.passage: AI-generated content can be inaccurate, misleading, or entirely fabricated (sometimes called “hallucinations”), and may contain copyrighted material.
units.why: The same sentence says AI content 'may contain copyrighted material', a copyright caution about AI output (P52) separate from the accuracy warning.

units.passage: Clarify who holds the rights to content generated by AI tools.
units.why: 'Clarify who holds the rights to content generated by AI tools' concerns ownership of AI output, P52.

units.passage: Ensure that output from AI tools do not infringe on existing copyright by generating content that closely replicates or derives from copyrighted materials without permission.
units.why: 'Ensure that output from AI tools do not infringe on existing copyright' is a copyright duty on AI output, P52.

units.passage: If AI-generated content is based on datasets or models using copyrighted materials, proper attribution or licensing agreements may be required.
units.why: 'proper attribution or licensing agreements may be required' for output based on copyrighted datasets is a licensing/attribution condition, P52 rather than P24 because it concerns copyright sources, not disclosing AI use.

units.passage: Confirm that any images or videos generated by AI tools are free from copyright issues, or ensure proper licensing and permissions are obtained.
units.why: 'Confirm that any images or videos generated by AI tools are free from copyright issues' is a copyright duty for AI media, P52.

units.passage: Disputes may arise over who owns IP developed with AI help (especially if multiple contributors are involved) and there is even an argument as to whether or not intellectual property generated by AI tools can even be protected.
units.why: Flags 'Disputes may arise over who owns IP developed with AI help'. Ownership of AI-assisted work is P52.

units.passage: Brandeis community members must adhere to applicable laws and legal obligations when using AI and take care to avoid infringing on the legal rights of others. This may include laws or regulations on intellectual property, FERPA and other privacy laws, and other regulations.
units.why: 'must adhere to applicable laws and legal obligations when using AI' with IP and FERPA named; legal and IP compliance fits P52 better than P50 because the passage is about legal rights.

units.passage: In addition, Brandeis community members must comply with applicable contracts, end user agreements, and other terms that relate to the use of AI tools.
units.why: Members 'must comply with applicable contracts, end user agreements, and other terms' of AI tools; terms of use, P52.

units.passage: Protecting Intellectual Property While AI has great potential for university research, Brown investigators contemplating using generative AI tools in their own research should be cognizant of the various intellectual property issues related to its use.
units.why: Brown investigators 'should be cognizant of the various intellectual property issues' of generative AI in research; copyright and IP of AI use is P52, directed to researchers (all).

units.passage: The applicability of copyright law, moral rights , and fair use to these tools is still under discussion.
units.policy: The applicability of copyright law, moral rights, and fair use to these tools is still under discussion.
units.why: "The applicability of copyright law, moral rights, and fair use to these tools is still under discussion" states legal uncertainty over AI use. P52 covers copyright and licensing.

units.passage: Some generative AI products, such as Adobe Firefly , prohibit users from uploading copyrighted materials without permission of the copyright holder.
units.why: Some products, such as Adobe Firefly, "prohibit users from uploading copyrighted materials without permission of the copyright holder", a tool-terms fact about copyright. P52 rather than P49 because the rule belongs to the tool, not the College.

units.passage: Generative AI content can be inaccurate, misleading, or entirely fabricated (sometimes called “hallucinations”) or may contain copyrighted material.
units.why: 'may contain copyrighted material' flags the copyright risk of AI output, which is P52 (licensing and copyright of output), informs.

units.passage: Unauthorized inclusion of others works; rights and attributions - In addition to including the works of others without authorization, some Gen AI software will imitate creators without clearly stating so and offering proper credit and attributions, and many artists, authors, programmers, and creators have discovered content generated by AI models that is nearly identical to their own. In many cases, there was never any authorization granted to use their works as part of the Gen AI software’s training data. This can be of particular concern when using AI generated content in research and academic work as it may include another person's work with incorrect or no citation and attribution.
units.why: The bullet on "Unauthorized inclusion of others works; rights and attributions" says models imitate creators without credit and may include others' work in research; this is a copyright and attribution concern, P52.

units.passage: Individuals should be familiar with the terms of use for the software which they are using.
units.why: "Individuals should be familiar with the terms of use for the software" is a should about licensing and terms (P52).

units.passage: Individuals are responsible for ensuring that AI generated content does not infringe on the intellectual property rights of third parties, includes proper citations, and aligns with the university’s policies and procedures.
units.why: Individuals must ensure AI content "does not infringe on the intellectual property rights of third parties" and aligns with policy; IP responsibility, P52, and the citation duty is coded separately.
units.fit_note: Coder A noted: also requires proper citations and alignment with university policies, beyond IP (the citation duty is coded as a separate P24 unit).

units.passage: You are responsible for the information you submit based on an AI query (for instance, that it does not violate intellectual property laws, or contain misinformation or unethical content). Your use of AI tools must be properly documented and cited in order to stay within university policies on academic integrity. Remember, AI is not likely to generate a response that would be seen as quality work and should be modified and improved. If AI is permitted and encouraged Example #1 You are welcome to use generative AI tools (such as ChatGPT, Google Gemini, Microsoft Copilot, Claude, etc.) in this class, and in some cases, you will be expected to do so. AI usage should be documented and cited [insert instructions or citation format]. You are responsible for respecting intellectual property and ensuring that any information generated by AI is accurate and ethical.
units.why: "responsible for respecting intellectual property" is an IP duty for AI use (P52).

units.passage: Not all generative AI responses are accurate, and some may violate intellectual property rights.
units.why: "some may violate intellectual property rights" names an IP risk of AI output, P52 as informs.

units.passage: If you choose to use AI during the course of your academic studies, please be aware that AI can produce responses that are not always accurate and/or may violate intellectual property rights.
units.why: AI responses "may violate intellectual property rights", an IP warning, P52.

units.passage: Submitting student work to anti-plagiarism software may violate students’ intellectual property rights.
units.why: The memo warns that uploading student work to a detector "may violate students' intellectual property rights" and the student "may lose ownership". This is about ownership of inputs, so P52 is nearest although it concerns student work rather than AI output.
units.fit_note: P52 covers ownership of AI inputs and outputs; this says student work uploaded to a detector may lose its student ownership.

units.passage: AI can also collect creative content like art and music and generate content that is based on a person’s work; it's important to be mindful of the potential for intellectual property loss as laws protecting content generated by AI are still evolving.
units.why: Users should be 'mindful of the potential for intellectual property loss' as laws on AI content evolve: P52.

units.passage: incorporate copyrighted material without appropriate attribution
units.policy: Generative AI tools sometimes incorporate copyrighted material without appropriate attribution.
units.why: "incorporate copyrighted material without appropriate attribution" names a copyright risk of AI output, P52.

units.passage: Responses from generative AI tools may contain content and materials from other authors and may be copyrighted.
units.why: 'may contain content and materials from other authors and may be copyrighted' is a general copyright fact about AI output, so P52, informs, general.

units.passage: AI systems or associated data cannot be used in ways that violate other university policy, applicable laws, other contracts that govern use of specific data (including license agreements governing library-provided information resources), or information security standards including but not limited to library licensed content, copyrighted materials created internal or external to Clark, or other community created intellectual property.
units.why: AI use cannot violate 'library licensed content, copyrighted materials' or community intellectual property, a copyright and licensing limit, so P52, must-not.

units.passage: AI outputs may incorporate or resemble copyrighted or proprietary content.
units.why: Legal risk that outputs "may incorporate or resemble copyrighted or proprietary content": P52.

units.passage: Specific prohibitions include illegal uploading of copyrighted materials.
units.why: Acceptable Use summary: 'Specific prohibitions include illegal uploading of copyrighted materials'; P52.

units.passage: Similarly, U.S. patent law requires a human inventor.
units.why: The memo states 'U.S. patent law requires a human inventor' and that copyright needs human creativity. This is about ownership of AI output, so P52, informs.

units.passage: The U.S. Copyright Office has clarified that to be eligible for copyright protection, a work must contain "sufficient human creativity.
units.why: To get copyright protection a work needs "sufficient human creativity", an ownership statement about AI output, P52.

units.passage: When you use AI to create a document or image, the output might unknowingly incorporate IP elements (photos and video, written pieces, audio, etc.) which may have been included in the data the tool trained from. This can lead to liability claims about whether your use of such material infringes upon another's intellectual property rights
units.why: Notes AI output "might unknowingly incorporate IP elements", an infringement risk statement, P52.

units.passage: When using AI, you are ultimately responsible for ensuring your output does not infringe on existing copyrights or other intellectual property protections.
units.why: The tip says 'you are ultimately responsible for ensuring your output does not infringe on existing copyrights'. It is a copyright duty on the user, so P52, must.

units.passage: You are also responsible to ensure that the information, data, or material you load or post on an AI platform is not intellectual property of another that you are providing without their consent.
units.why: The memo says 'You are also responsible to ensure that the information, data, or material you load or post on an AI platform is not intellectual property of another'. It is a duty about third-party IP and consent, so P52 must; it limits what is loaded, so restrict.

units.passage: Training AI on pirated content is generally not fair use.
units.why: The memo states 'Training AI on pirated content is generally not fair use.' It is a copyright fact about AI training, so P52, informs.

units.passage: Students retain ownership of their original work except where University policy, employment agreements, sponsored research agreements, or other applicable law or contractual obligations provide otherwise.
units.why: "Students retain ownership of their original work" states who owns student work, which is about ownership of AI inputs and outputs and IP (P52).

units.passage: Users of GenAI tools must perform due diligence to ensure that outputs do not infringe copyright.
units.why: "Users of GenAI tools must perform due diligence to ensure that outputs do not infringe copyright" is a duty about copyright of AI output (P52).

units.passage: Faculty, staff, and students using these tools must read and understand the AI tool vendor’s policies and become familiar with the limitations of use and how the vendor plans to store, process, or handle CU’s data
units.why: "must read and understand the AI tool vendor’s policies" makes faculty, staff and students check the vendor's terms of use, P52.
units.fit_note: Concerns vendor terms of use and data handling more than copyright or ownership. / Also asks users to understand how the vendor stores and handles CU data.

units.passage: Some generative AIs were trained on the work of authors, journalists, artists, or musicians who did not give the companies permission to use their work for this purpose. Artists, writers, comedians and companies like The New York Times and Disney have filed lawsuits against various generative AI companies alleging that they have violated their rights as creators.
units.why: Lawsuits alleging generative AI was "trained on the work of authors" without permission raise copyright concerns: P52.

units.passage: When using generative AI tools, consider the ethical implications of uploading another author or artist’s work or prompting the AI to produce outputs based on copyrighted characters.
units.policy: When using generative AI tools, consider the ethical implications of uploading another author or artist's work or prompting the AI to produce outputs based on copyrighted characters.
units.why: It asks students to "consider the ethical implications of uploading another author or artist’s work" to AI, a copyright concern, so P52 (not P49, which is about course materials).
units.fit_note: Frames copyright as an ethical consideration, not a legal rule or permission. Asks for consideration, not a ban on uploading protected works.

units.passage: For information about AI and copyright, see this quick reference guide from Academic Affairs
units.why: "For information about AI and copyright, see this quick reference guide" points to IP guidance: P52 informs.

units.passage: For information about AI and copyright, see this quick reference guide from Academic Affairs
units.why: Points students to a copyright quick reference guide: P52 informs.

units.passage: The United States Copyright Office published guidance on copyright in January 2025.
units.why: The Copyright Office "published guidance on copyright in January 2025" is pointed to in the discussion of AI and copyright. A reference to copyright of AI material, so P52, though no rule is stated.
units.fit_note: Only points to external copyright guidance without stating a rule.

units.passage: GAI tools also have implications for intellectual property rights.
units.why: The report says 'GAI tools also have implications for intellectual property rights'. Ownership and IP risk, so P52.

units.passage: While there are many opportunities, concerns exist around ethical attribution of sources and copyright violations.
units.why: For creative courses the report notes 'concerns exist around ethical attribution of sources and copyright violations'. Copyright and attribution of AI output, so P52.

units.passage: Where GenAI has been used collaboratively within a research group or lab, graduate students must ensure that in addition to crediting all parties appropriately, IP contributions should be documented to reflect the use of AI tools.
units.why: Where AI is used in a research group, "IP contributions should be documented to reflect the use of AI tools" concerns ownership of AI inputs and outputs (P52).

units.passage: Unauthorized disclosure of sensitive information to cloud AI platforms may compromise future publication and patent rights.
units.policy: Unauthorized disclosure of sensitive information to cloud AI platforms may compromise future publication and patent rights.
units.why: "may compromise future publication and patent rights" is an IP-risk statement (P52).

units.passage: Where GenAI has been used collaboratively within a research group or lab, Thayer students must ensure that, in addition to crediting all parties appropriately, IP contributions should be documented to reflect the use of AI tools.
units.why: Where AI is used in a research group, "IP contributions should be documented to reflect the use of AI tools" concerns ownership of AI inputs and outputs (P52).

units.passage: Unauthorized disclosure of sensitive information to cloud AI platforms may compromise future publication and patent rights.
units.policy: Unauthorized disclosure of sensitive information to cloud AI platforms may compromise future publication and patent rights.
units.why: "may compromise future publication and patent rights" is an IP-risk statement (P52).

units.passage: Additionally, users of generative AI tools are cautioned that the copyright implications of works created in whole or in part using AI technology are uncertain and have not been resolved through relevant lawmaking or legal processes.
units.why: Users "are cautioned that the copyright implications of works created in whole or in part using AI technology are uncertain": a copyright and ownership caution (P52).

units.passage: Individuals creating works for which the individual and/or the college may assert copyright privileges (see, e.g., the College Intellectual Property Policy ) are advised to seek advice on the current state of AI and copyright before using AI in their work.
units.why: Creators of works the college may claim copyright in "are advised to seek advice on the current state of AI and copyright before using AI": advice on copyright of AI output (P52).

units.passage: One helpful source of guidance is the U.S. Copyright Office’s resources on copyright and AI
units.why: Points to US Copyright Office resources as helpful guidance on AI and copyright, P52.

units.passage: In violation of the University’s student and faculty handbooks and policies or applicable laws, including laws governing intellectual property.
units.why: AI content "in violation of ... laws governing intellectual property" flags IP risk of outputs, so P52; informs.

units.passage: Users who paraphrase or borrow ideas from the output of generative AI tools must confirm its accuracy and that they are not plagiarizing another party’s existing work product or violating another party’s intellectual property rights.
units.why: Users who paraphrase or borrow ideas "must confirm its accuracy and that they are not plagiarizing another party's existing work product or violating ... intellectual property rights", an IP and accuracy duty; P52 chosen because the plagiarism and IP part is the distinctive content.
units.fit_note: Also requires an accuracy check; P52 is about licensing and ownership.

units.passage: and should also follow copyright and licensing requirements.
units.why: Faculty "should also follow copyright and licensing requirements" when using AI, so P52; should.

units.passage: If Generative AI is given access to confidential information or trade secrets, the University may lose its intellectual property (“IP”) rights to that information and the information may be disclosed to unauthorized third parties through their independent use of the Generative AI technology.
units.why: Risk bullet: with confidential information "the University may lose its intellectual property (IP) rights", an IP and confidentiality risk, so P52; informs.
units.fit_note: Risk is loss of IP rights and disclosure to third parties through use of the tool.

units.passage: Generative AI outputs may violate the IP rights of others and might not themselves be protected by IP laws.
units.why: Risk bullet: "Generative AI outputs may violate the IP rights of others and might not themselves be protected by IP laws" is about copyright of outputs, so P52; informs.

units.passage: If the output includes any quote, paraphrase, or borrowed ideas from the output of Generative AI tools or services, University Users must confirm that the output is accurate and not plagiarize another party’s existing work or otherwise violate another party’s intellectual property rights.
units.why: Where output includes "any quote, paraphrase, or borrowed ideas", users "must confirm that the output is accurate and not plagiarize"; an IP and accuracy duty, so P52 (the plagiarism and IP part is distinctive).
units.fit_note: Also requires an accuracy check.

units.passage: Entering copyrighted material into a Generative AI tool or service may effectively result in the creation of a digital copy, which is a copyright violation.
units.why: "Entering copyrighted material into a Generative AI tool or service may effectively result in the creation of a digital copy, which is a copyright violation" explains the copyright risk of inputs, P52, informational.

units.passage: In addition, entering research into Generative AI tool or service could constitute premature disclosure, compromising invention patentability.
units.why: Footnote: "entering research into Generative AI tool or service could constitute premature disclosure, compromising invention patentability" warns about IP and research disclosure, so P52; informs.

units.passage: Users may not use AI tools or services to infringe copyright or other intellectual property rights.
units.why: Footnote: "Users may not use AI tools or services to infringe copyright or other intellectual property rights" is a copyright ban, so P52; must-not.

units.passage: Generative AI-produced content may be biased, inaccurate, completely fabricated, or contain copyright-protected or proprietary information
units.why: Notes output may 'contain copyright-protected or proprietary information', a licensing and IP concern about AI output.

units.passage: It is not clear who owns AI content and if it can be copyrighted
units.why: Raises ownership and copyright uncertainty about AI output: P52.

units.passage: AI-generated content may inadvertently plagiarize from copyrighted sources, especially in art and text generation
units.why: Warns of copyright plagiarism in AI output: P52.

units.passage: East Carolina University encourages exploration of these products or services, but individuals must remain cognizant of data being provided to these tools, as well as abide by copyright laws, compliance regulations, Employee Code of Conduct, and Student Code of Conduct.
units.why: Individuals must 'abide by copyright laws' when using these tools. Copyright compliance of AI use fits P52 (licensing and copyright). Final codes follow the resolution_why.

units.passage: Their basic position as of mid-March 2023 is that texts and images solely or primarily generated by AI are not eligible for copyright protection; texts and images that originated in AI but have had significant authorial contributions may be eligible on a case-by-case basis.
units.why: States the Copyright Office position that AI-generated texts 'are not eligible for copyright protection'. Copyright of AI output, P52.

units.passage: outlines their perspective and gives instructions on filling out the copyright registration forms to acknowledge the role of AI in any work being submitted.
units.why: Federal Register guidance 'gives instructions on filling out the copyright registration forms to acknowledge the role of AI'. Copyright registration disclosure, P52.

units.passage: Shall not utilize GAI to present a work as their own in violation of another individual’s intellectual property rights
units.why: Users 'Shall not utilize GAI to present a work as their own in violation of another individual's intellectual property rights'; this is about IP, so P52 rather than P19.

units.passage: Shall follow all copyright laws;
units.why: 2.5 'Shall follow all copyright laws' is a copyright rule: P52.

units.passage: Ensure AI use complies with copyright, intellectual property, and privacy laws.
units.why: "Ensure AI use complies with copyright, intellectual property, and privacy laws" covers IP and legal compliance, P52.

units.passage: ignore privacy, copyright, or intellectual property concerns
units.why: 'ignore privacy, copyright, or intellectual property concerns' tells users not to disregard IP; copyright and ownership of AI input and output is P52.

units.why: Students should be 'cautiously selective about the number and size of code snippets' because of 'software license restrictions' and copyright: P52.

units.passage: Members of the Penn community should adhere to established principles of respect for intellectual property, particularly copyrights when considering the creation of new data sets for training AI models.
units.why: "adhere to established principles of respect for intellectual property, particularly copyrights" when creating training data sets is a copyright and IP rule (P52).

units.passage: Avoid uploading confidential and/or proprietary information to AI platforms prior to seeking patent or copyright protection, as doing so could jeopardize IP rights.
units.why: "Avoid uploading confidential and/or proprietary information to AI platforms prior to seeking patent or copyright protection" protects IP rights, so P52.
units.fit_note: Rule is about preserving patent and copyright protection of unpublished IP, not licensing of AI output.
